content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics, specifically focusing on rapid diagnostic methods for TB detection. This handbook, updated in 2021, provides detailed guidance on implementing WHO-recommended diagnostic tests and algorithms for TB and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The handbook outlines the need for universal access to drug-susceptibility testing (DST) for all TB patients, particularly for rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH) resistance. It highlights the critical role of rapid molecular diagnostic tests, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), in detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and drug resistance. These tests are recommended as the initial diagnostic approach to minimize delays in treatment initiation. The WHO has transitioned to a class-based recommendation system for diagnostic tools, which evaluates groups of products with similar characteristics and performance rather than individual products. This approach aims to enhance competitiveness in price, quality, and service. The handbook also introduces new classes of diagnostic technologies, including moderate-complexity automated NAATs for detecting TB and resistance to RIF and INH, as well as high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance detection. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay, a cartridge-based automated test using real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), is recommended as an initial diagnostic test for TB and RIF resistance in adults and children with pulmonary TB symptoms. It is also advised for use in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for diagnosing TB meningitis and in other specimens for extrapulmonary TB. The updated Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay offers improved sensitivity and a lower limit of detection, making it suitable for cases with very low bacterial loads. Conventional diagnostic methods, such as sputum-smear microscopy and culture, remain in use in many high-burden settings but are less sensitive and slower compared to molecular tests. WHO recommends transitioning from microscopy to rapid molecular diagnostic tests for initial TB diagnosis. Culture methods, while still important for monitoring treatment response and diagnosing pediatric or extrapulmonary TB, are not widely used as primary diagnostic tools due to their cost, infrastructure requirements, and long turnaround times. The handbook also provides practical steps for implementing new diagnostic tools, including considerations for laboratory capacity, quality assurance, biosafety, and human resources. In summary, the WHO operational handbook serves as a comprehensive guide for health ministries, program managers, laboratory personnel, and other stakeholders involved in TB diagnostics. It aims to improve TB detection and treatment outcomes through the adoption of rapid, accurate, and accessible diagnostic technologies.
